title: Unseen mass or a wrong law?
teaches: Why galaxies and clusters seem to hold far more mass than we can see, the case for dark matter against a change in the law of gravity, and why the answer is still open

parts.title: A cluster that should fly apart

blocks.text: In 1933 Fritz Zwicky, a brilliant, abrasive Swiss astronomer at Caltech (the same Zwicky who predicted neutron stars in *Little green men*), measured the speeds of galaxies in the Coma cluster, a swarm of more than a thousand galaxies about 320 million light years away. They were moving fast, around a thousand kilometres a second. A cluster can only hold on to galaxies that fast if it has enough mass to pull them back, and adding up the light of all its galaxies gave nothing like enough. By Zwicky's sums the cluster needed hundreds of times more mass than its stars could account for. He called the missing stuff *dunkle Materie*, dark matter.

Zwicky was disliked, and his numbers were rough, and for forty years hardly anyone took the problem seriously. It was put down to bad measurements or some untidiness in clusters. Then it turned up again, in ordinary galaxies, where it couldn't be ignored.

In the Solar System, the further a planet is from the Sun, the slower it goes: Mercury races round at 48 kilometres a second, Neptune plods at 5. Nearly all the mass is in the middle, so the pull fades with distance and the outer planets need less speed to stay in orbit. A spiral galaxy's light is concentrated towards its middle too, so its outer stars ought to orbit more slowly, the same way. Plot how fast things orbit against distance from the centre, a graph called a **rotation curve**, and you'd expect it to rise and then fall away.

In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford at the Carnegie Institution in Washington, using a sensitive new spectrograph Ford had built, measured the speeds of stars and gas across spiral galaxy after spiral galaxy, by the Doppler shifts of their light. The curves didn't fall. They rose and then stayed flat, out to the faintest edges of the starlight. At about the same time, the Dutch astronomer Albert Bosma used radio telescopes to follow the cold hydrogen gas that extends far beyond the stars. Out there, where there is almost no light at all, the gas was still going round just as fast.

blocks.caption: A spiral galaxy's rotation curve: orbit speed against distance from the centre. The dots are measurements; the line is what the mass you include predicts.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then add unseen mass until the prediction fits

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The outer parts of galaxies orbit too fast for the mass we can see. Either there is a lot of unseen mass, or gravity behaves differently far out.

blocks.text: This is the fork you met in *A planet found with a pen*. When Uranus strayed from its path, Le Verrier trusted the law of gravity and found an unseen mass: Neptune. When Mercury strayed, he tried the same thing and invented Vulcan, but the real answer was a wrong law, fixed by Einstein. The galaxies are straying. Which kind of problem is this?

The Neptune answer is **dark matter**: mass that gives out no light and is felt only by its pull, gathered in a great round halo enveloping each galaxy and extending far past its stars. To flatten the curves, a galaxy like ours needs several times as much of it as all its stars and gas put together.

The Mercury answer came in 1983 from the Israeli physicist Mordehai Milgrom. Perhaps, he said, gravity changes its behaviour when it gets very weak, as it is in the outskirts of galaxies, fading more slowly with distance than Newton's law says. He called it Modified Newtonian Dynamics, MOND. It is a simple rule, and it predicts the rotation curves of individual galaxies remarkably well, often better than dark matter does, from their visible mass alone. It cannot be dismissed. But a law has to work everywhere, and the hardest tests are on bigger scales.

Most of the ordinary matter in a cluster of galaxies is not in the galaxies at all. It is in thin gas between them, heated to tens of millions of degrees, glowing in X-rays. And the total mass of a cluster can be mapped independently, by the way it bends the light of more distant galaxies behind it: the gravitational lensing of *The Sun bends starlight*.

In 2006 astronomers looked at a pair of clusters, nicknamed the Bullet Cluster, that collided head-on about 150 million years ago. The galaxies, mostly empty space with far apart stars, sailed past one another. The hot gas clouds of the two clusters slammed into each other, slowed, and were left behind in the middle. So most of the ordinary matter is in the middle. But the lensing map shows most of the mass is out with the galaxies, on either side, having passed straight through like the galaxies did.

blocks.caption: The Bullet Cluster, drawn simply. The hot gas (pink) was left in the middle; the mass, mapped by lensing (blue), went on with the galaxies.

blocks.text: If gravity simply followed the ordinary matter under a different law, it should be centred on the gas. It isn't. Something with mass, which doesn't collide like gas does, passed through. Modified-gravity theories have struggled to explain this without adding unseen matter of their own.

In 1986 Valérie de Lapparent, Margaret Geller and John Huchra at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA) measured the redshifts, and so the distances, of a thousand galaxies in a thin slice of the sky. They expected them to be scattered fairly evenly. Instead the galaxies lay on the walls of enormous empty bubbles, like the film of a mass of soap suds, with a cluster in the middle making a shape like a stick figure. The universe on its largest scales is a web of walls and threads round huge voids.

blocks.caption: A slice of the universe, as mapped in 1986, with us at the bottom point. Each dot is a galaxy. The Coma cluster makes the stick figure's body.

blocks.text: Now remember the afterglow of *Why is the night sky dark?*: smooth to one part in 100,000. Gravity makes denser patches pull in more matter and grow denser still, but slowly. Since the afterglow was released the universe has stretched about 1,100 times, and ripples of ordinary matter grow roughly in step with it. One part in 100,000 times 1,100 is about one percent. That isn't a web of galaxies. It isn't even one galaxy.

blocks.caption: How much denser than average the dense patches of the universe are, from 10,000 years after the start to today, in a simplified picture: ordinary matter alone (grey), and with dark matter (blue).
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then add dark matter until galaxies can form

blocks.text: Dark matter solves it. Light pushes ordinary matter around, and in the hot early universe that push kept its ripples from growing. Dark matter feels gravity but not light, so its clumps had been growing for hundreds of thousands of years before the afterglow, and were far deeper than the afterglow shows. When the ordinary matter was freed, it fell into wells that were already there.

Could the dark matter just be ordinary atoms that are hard to see: dim stars, lost planets, cold gas? Two separate measurements say no. The first is **deuterium**, heavy hydrogen, made only in the first few minutes of the universe. How much of it was made depends sensitively on how much ordinary matter there was, and the amount measured in pristine gas clouds says ordinary matter is about a sixth of all matter. The second is the exact pattern of ripples in the afterglow, which gives the same answer. About five-sixths of the matter in the universe is something else.

So what is it? Most physicists think it is some kind of particle not yet discovered, which barely interacts with anything except by gravity. Detectors deep underground, tanks of liquid xenon shielded from cosmic rays by a mile of rock, have waited for decades for one to bump into an atom. The Large Hadron Collider at CERN has looked for signs of them being made. None has been found. The searches have ruled out many of the most popular ideas, and others remain.

Unseen mass explains a great deal: rotation curves, the Bullet Cluster, the web of galaxies, the afterglow's ripples. A modified law explains rotation curves very neatly and the rest badly. But until someone catches a dark matter particle, or finds a law that does everything, the honest answer to this lesson's title is that most of the evidence points to unseen mass, and no one knows what it is.

blocks.caption: Six questions on dark matter
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: In the Solar System, outer planets orbit more slowly. Why was the same expected for stars in the outskirts of galaxies?
choices: Most of a galaxy's visible mass is near its centre, so the pull should fade further out
items.why: With most of the mass in the middle, less speed is needed to stay in orbit further out, as for the planets.

items.ask: A galaxy's rotation curve stays flat far beyond its starlight. What does dark matter say?
choices: There is a lot of unseen mass in a halo that extends beyond the stars
The outer stars are being pushed
items.why: Extra mass further out keeps the pull strong enough to hold fast-moving outer stars in orbit.

items.ask: In the Bullet Cluster, why does it matter that the mass is out with the galaxies, not with the hot gas?
choices: Most of the ordinary matter is in the gas, so the mass can't simply be ordinary matter under a different law
It shows the clusters are moving apart
items.why: If gravity just followed ordinary matter, it would be centred on the gas. Instead, something massive that doesn't collide passed straight through.

items.ask: The afterglow's ripples were one part in 100,000. Why couldn't ordinary matter alone grow them into galaxies?
choices: They grow only about as fast as the universe stretches, so by now they would only have reached about one percent
items.why: 1,100 times one part in 100,000 is about one percent. Dark matter, untouched by light's push, had a head start.

items.ask: How do we know dark matter isn't just dim stars and planets?
choices: Deuterium from the first minutes, and the afterglow's ripples, both say ordinary matter is only about a sixth of all matter
Planets would be seen by lensing
items.why: Both measurements fix the amount of ordinary matter, and it falls far short of the total.

items.ask: Which is the Mercury-style answer to the flat rotation curves?
choices: A change to the law of gravity at very weak pulls (MOND)
items.why: Mercury's riddle was solved by a new law, not a new planet. MOND is that kind of answer for galaxies.

summary: **Zwicky, 1933.** The Coma cluster's galaxies move too fast for the mass we can see.
**Flat rotation curves.** Rubin, Ford and Bosma: stars and gas far out in spiral galaxies orbit as fast as those further in.
**Unseen mass or a wrong law?** Dark matter (the Neptune answer) or modified gravity, MOND (the Mercury answer).
**The Bullet Cluster.** Lensing shows the mass passed through with the galaxies, while the gas stayed behind.
**Galaxies needed a head start.** Ripples of one part in 100,000 grow too slowly without dark matter.
**It isn't ordinary atoms.** Deuterium and the afterglow say ordinary matter is about a sixth of all matter.
**Still unseen.** Decades of searches have caught no dark matter particle; the question is open.
